opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's really a question of sequencing more than anything else. The US is, by a wide margin, the epicenter of AI right now. The largest model developers, the hyperscalers, the neoclouds, the enterprises that are actually deploying these models at scale, the vast majority of them are here. So if you're a company like ours, building silicon for inference, you have to go where the demand is most concentrated and where the most sophisticated customers are. Those customers push you hardest, they give you the most demanding workloads, and they validate your technology in a way that then makes it much easier to go elsewhere.

There's also a practical point. As a startup, you have finite resources. You can't be everywhere at once. You can't have deep engineering engagements with twenty different sovereign AI initiatives in parallel while you're also trying to land and ramp your first major deployments. So focus matters. We'd rather go deep with a smaller number of customers and get it right than spread ourselves thin.

That said, we're very aware of what's happening globally. Sovereign AI is real. Countries in the Middle East, in Europe, in Asia, they all recognize that compute is strategic infrastructure, almost like energy or telecom, and they want control over it. And frankly, a lot of that build-out is going to be inference-heavy, because once you've trained or licensed a model, the ongoing cost is serving it to your population, your enterprises, your government services. That's exactly where we play. So it's not that we're ignoring those markets. It's that the US is where we prove the technology at scale, and that becomes the foundation for going international. I'd expect our footprint outside the US to grow meaningfully over the next couple of years.

And there's a geopolitical layer too. Export controls and policy are shaping where advanced compute can go, so being anchored in the US and aligned with that ecosystem gives us a stable base as the rules evolve.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the US is where the company proves its technology before expanding internationally, but it does not predict that opportunities will emerge there before diffusing specifically to Global South countries.

r002.rationale: The candidate says demanding US customers validate the technology and that this helps the company go elsewhere, but it does not state that resolving AI deployment and application-fit questions is a prerequisite for diffusion into sovereign and enterprise applications.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, I think the simple answer is that the US is still where the largest, most sophisticated buyers of AI inference are, and where the decisions about what the next generation of infrastructure looks like are actually being made. The hyperscalers are here, the frontier labs are here, the enterprises with the biggest deployment budgets are here. If you want to prove that a new architecture works at scale, you want to prove it with the customers who are pushing hardest, and today those customers are disproportionately American.

There's also a practical dimension around the ecosystem. When you're building silicon, you're not just building a chip, you're building the software stack, the developer tooling, the system integrations, the partnerships with OEMs and cloud providers. That ecosystem is deepest in the US. The feedback loops are faster. You can sit down with a customer in Santa Clara or Seattle and iterate on a design in a way that's much harder to do across time zones and regulatory boundaries.

And frankly, there's a policy element. Compute has become strategic, and the US is investing heavily in domestic AI infrastructure. Being a company that can serve that need, with a supply chain and a product roadmap that aligns with where the government and the industry want to go, matters.

That said, I wouldn't characterize it as US to the exclusion of everyone else. We're a global company, we have teams in India and elsewhere, and we absolutely see demand coming from sovereign AI efforts in Europe, the Middle East, and Asia. Inference, in particular, needs to happen close to where the data and the users are, so by definition it's going to be distributed geographically. But you have to sequence these things. You win the anchor market first, you build credibility with the most demanding customers, and then you take that proof point to everyone else. For us, the US is that anchor.

r001.rationale: The response says the US is the anchor market and that its proof point can later be taken to “everyone else,” but it does not specifically predict diffusion to countries in the Global South.

r002.rationale: It describes proving the architecture at scale before expanding, but does not state that resolving AI deployment and application-fit questions is a prerequisite for diffusion into sovereign and enterprise applications.

astra-6.text:
We prioritize the US because that’s where we see the greatest concentration of customers building and deploying AI at scale. Being close to those customers helps us understand what they need from the infrastructure—whether that’s performance, power efficiency, or cost—and focus our efforts accordingly.

That doesn’t mean the opportunity is limited to the US. As countries build their own AI infrastructure, they’ll need efficient compute as well. For us, it’s a question of sequencing: establish ourselves in the US while building relationships that allow us to serve those other markets as they develop.

r001.rationale: The response describes establishing a US presence before serving other markets, but does not predict that AI opportunities will emerge in the US before diffusing to the Global South.

r002.rationale: It mentions understanding infrastructure needs such as performance, power efficiency, and cost, but does not present resolving deployment or application-fit questions as a prerequisite for diffusion into sovereign and enterprise applications.

That doesn’t mean the opportunity elsewhere is any less important. As countries build their own AI infrastructure, they’ll need efficient compute as well. But we have to be deliberate about where we put our resources, and the US is our starting point.
